newsitem.title: USA: Record yields boost US wheat outlook, despite spring freeze.
newsitem.headline: Record yields boost US wheat outlook, despite spring freeze.

text.p: U.S. winter wheat yields will hit record levels this year despite a hard April freeze that many analysts thought would cripple the crop, the U.S. Agriculture Department said on Friday.

Based on July 1 conditions, the department estimated the U.S. winter wheat harvest at 1.78 billion bushels, up 11 percent from its June estimate and 20 percent from a year ago. Yields were pegged at a record 42.8 bushels per acre, up 5.6 bushels from last year.

Kansas, one of the states hardest hit by the freeze, is now expected to produce 449.4 million bushels, up from last month's estimate of 363.8 million and last year's 255.2 million, which was reduced by drought.

The department forecast the total U.S. wheat crop, which also includes spring wheat, at 2.43 billion bushels -- the largest crop in five years. The department's season-average price estimate for the 1997 wheat crop is now $3.40 per bushel, down 95 cents from last year.

The Agriculture Department pegged the U.S. soybean crop at 2.69 billion bushels, up sharply from last year. Farmers responded to high soybean prices this spring by planting the most soybean acres in 15 years.

However, the increased soybean plantings came at the expense of corn. The department estimated this year's corn crop at 9.70 billion bushels, down from its June estimate to reflect the lower-than-expected planting. The crop is still expected to about 400 million bushels bigger than last year.
